name: Maore Comorian
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file
sweep_summary: maor1244 is not in the catalog. Six Glottolog title hits, none with an open copy: Philippson 1988 (Études océan indien 9, print-only; covers 'all Comorian dialects' but on Anjouan data per Lafon), Philippson 2005 (Tervuren, print-only; the one item with explicit first-hand Shimaore prosody, known only through Patin's quotations of pp. 212-213: phrase-level pitch accent, residual lexical marked/unmarked contrast in short phrases, default penultimate foot in longer phrases, antepenult tone at utterance level), Jouannet 1989 (Shingazidja; read via Lafon's 1991 review), Ahmed-Chamanga 1986 and Jaffar 1992 (both Anjouan/Ndzwani, print-only or unlocatable), and Philippson 1991 (thesis read in full from the author-posted PDF: Comorian = purely accentual, treated only through Ndzuani, obligatory penultimate feet, no Shimaore data). Semantic Scholar and Google Books APIs were rate-limited; HAL and OpenEdition are behind Anubis from our machine. Best first-hand Shimaore statement remains Rombi 1983: 61-62 (page images re-read this sweep): stress on the penultimate syllable, shifting with locative/extension suffixes and prefixes, realised by pitch, with tone vestigial (p. 63). Acquisition priorities: Philippson 2005 (high), Philippson 1988 (high), Madi 2005 Lyon 2 thesis full text (not a title hit but claims 'accent libre'; server unreachable). Everything with and updated.

new_statements.quote: 1.3. L'ACCENT TONIQUE. Il se manifeste par la hauteur vocalique et par une articulation plus ferme. a) les polysyllabiques. L'accent tombe sur l'avant-dernière syllabe, exemples : 'da-go "village", dzi-'vu-zi "plume", 'nyu-mba "maison". L'adjonction d'un locatif ou d'une extension verbale entraîne un déplacement de l'accent tonique vers la droite, exemples : 'nyu-mba "maison" / nyu-'mba-ni "dans la maison" ; 'a-mba "dire" / a-'mbi-a "dire à". b) les monosyllabiques. Ils sont accentués. L'adjonction d'un préfixe entraîne un déplacement de l'accent vers la gauche, exemple : 'ji "voix" (sing.), 'ma-ji "voix" (pl.).
new_statements.translation: 1.3. WORD STRESS (accent tonique). It is manifested by vowel pitch and a firmer articulation. a) polysyllables: stress falls on the penultimate syllable, e.g. 'da-go 'village', dzi-'vu-zi 'feather', 'nyu-mba 'house'. Adding a locative or a verbal extension shifts the stress to the right: 'nyu-mba 'house' / nyu-'mba-ni 'in the house'; 'a-mba 'say' / a-'mbi-a 'say to'. b) monosyllables: they are stressed. Adding a prefix shifts the stress to the left: 'ji 'voice' (sg.), 'ma-ji 'voices' (pl.).
new_statements.citation: Rombi, Marie-Françoise. 1983. Le shimaore (île de Mayotte, Comores): première approche d'un parler de la langue comorienne. Paris: SELAF (Peeters), 266 pp. [HAL hal-00439181v2]
new_statements.locator: § 1.3 'L'accent tonique', pp. 61-62 (pdf pp. 59-60 of the HAL scan); tone caveats § 1.5 'Les tons', pp. 62-64
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (a pitch-plus-articulatory prominence) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, and it re-computes when suffixes/prefixes are added, so the penult of the derived word carries it (nyumba > nyumbáni; ji > máji). Monosyllables are stressed. All syllables are open (§1.4), so no weight sensitivity is at stake.
new_statements.exceptions: Rombi §1.5 (pp. 62-64): Comorian tone is 'vestigial en shimaore'; a small minority of the youngest informants keep tonal oppositions, lexical (maži 'water' vs mažÍ 'voice' cl.6; tsi 'eyebrow' vs tsÍ 'country') and grammatical (EPD vs copula, ligari lÁdagoni vs ligari la dagoni; accomplished tsisómó vs habitual negative tsisómo); older speakers give the impression of a tone language but analysis was impossible on the corpus; p. 64: 'n'a été vérifié... qu'avec deux informateurs sur six'. Later work disputes the plain penult rule: Madi 2005 (abstract only) says Shimaore is 'à accent libre alors que le swahili est à accent fixe'; Philippson 2005: 212-213, as quoted by Patin 2018/2022, keeps tone patterns on short phrases (ɓawá dziɗu 'black wing' vs ɓawa pána 'broad wing') and derives a left-dominant binary foot over the last two syllables (final extrametrical) only for phonological phrases of more than two tone domains, with 'one tone on the antepenult' at utterance level (riudzu maʒwai máili). Treat Rombi's rule as the default/citation-form pattern with a residual lexical accent contrast.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms (nouns, verbs, monosyllables with and without affixes); Rombi separates phrase-level intonemes (interrogation, insistence) in §1.5 and calls the word accent 'démarcatif de mot'. Description of Shimaore of Mayotte from Mahorais (and Mozambique-resident Mahorais) informants; Rombi & Alexandre-style INALCO Bantu framework.
new_statements.identity_note: Rombi 1983 describes Shimaore of Mayotte = maor1244 exactly (Glottolog names: Maore Comorian / Shimaore / Mahorais). Sibling varieties on file are ngaz1238 (Shingazidja) and mwal1237 (Shimwali); the Patin papers and Lafon review used here are primarily about Shingazidja and only quote Philippson 2005 on Shimaore second-hand. Rombi's informants were Mahorais (some resident in Mozambique); she notes (p. 64) that her tone observations rest on 2 of 6 informants, and calls tone 'vestigial' in Shimaore versus better preserved in Shimwali/Shindzuani.

new_statements.translation: 1.3 Word stress. It is manifested by vowel pitch and by a firmer articulation. a) Polysyllables: stress falls on the penultimate syllable, e.g. 'dago 'village', dzi'vuzi 'feather', 'nyumba 'house'. Adding a locative or a verbal extension shifts the stress one syllable to the right: 'nyumba 'house' / nyu'mbani 'in the house'; 'amba 'say' / a'mbia 'say to'. b) Monosyllables are stressed. Adding a prefix shifts the stress to the left: 'ji 'voice' (sg.) / 'maji 'voices' (pl.).
new_statements.citation: Rombi, Marie-Françoise (1983). Le shimaore (île de Mayotte, Comores): première approche d'un parler de la langue comorienne. Paris: SELAF (Langues et cultures africaines 2), 266 pp. HAL hal-00439181v2.
new_statements.locator: §1.3 'L'accent tonique', pp. 61-62 (pdf pp. 59-60); cf. §1.5 'Les tons', p. 63
new_statements.reading: First-hand description of Shimaore (Mayotte) with fixed, weight-insensitive penultimate word stress realised chiefly by pitch; the shift examples show it is computed on the derived word (locative -ni, extensions, prefixes). Rombi p. 63 adds that Shimaore's suprasegmental system is 'très proche de celui du swahili : accent démarcatif de mot' and that lexical tone is vestigial (kept only by a minority of informants; verified with two of six informants, p. 64). This is the only first-hand Shimaore stress statement read in this sweep. Caveats to record alongside it: Philippson 2005: 212-213 (unobtained, quoted by Patin) analyses Shimaore as a phrase-level pitch-accent system with a residual lexical marked/unmarked contrast in short phrases (ɓawá dziɗu vs ɓawa pána) and a default penultimate foot in longer ones; Madi 2005 (thesis abstract only, full text unreachable) calls Shimaore 'à accent libre'. A catalog entry should code fixed penultimate as the word-level default while flagging the residual-tone/phrasal overlay.

sources.citation: Patin, Cédric. 2022. The prosody of Shingazidja relatives: an update. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus (SPIL Plus), pp. ~172-173 of the issue (quoting Philippson 2005: 212-213 on Shimaore)
sources.note: Second-hand on Shimaore: 'Describing Shimaore... Philippson (2005: 213) writes: "If the [Phonological Phrase] comprises more than two [tone] domains, domain brackets will be erased, the final syllable will be made extrametrical, and a left-dominant binary foot constructed from right to left over the last two syllables"' (i.e. penultimate prominence at phrase level); short phrases keep tone patterns like Shingazidja: ɓawa pána 'broad wing', ɓawá dziɗu 'black wing'; tsisihaŋgiha ɓárua 'I am not writing a letter'.

sources.citation: Patin, Cédric. 2018. From tones to accents: the case of Shingazidja. Proceedings TAL 2018 (ISCA), p. 2 (citing Philippson 2005: 212-213)
sources.note: Second-hand: Shingazidja 'is closely related to languages that have lost their tones, such as another Comorian language, Shimaore [Philippson 2005]'; 'In Shimaore... rules similar in nature to those of Shingazidja apply to nouns or short phrases in isolation (ɓawá "wing" > ɓawa pána, ɓawá dziɗu — [9, p. 213]), but not at the utterance level, where only one tone emerges on the antepenult ([9, p. 212])': riudzu maʒwai máili 'We bought two eggs'.

sources.citation: Lafon, Michel. 1991. Review article / compte-rendu de Jouannet, Francis 1989, Des tons à l'accent: essai sur l'accentuation du comorien. Swahili Language and Society: Notes and News 8: 45-64 (HAL halshs-00078493)
sources.note: Mostly about Shingazidja. Summarises Rombi 1983: 63 (tone gradient across the four islands, 'vestigial en shimaore'); reports the Ahmed-Chamanga & Philippson metrical analysis of Comorian as marked vs unmarked syllables with 'accent pénultième par défaut en cas d'absence totale de syllabe marquée', Jouannet's noun classes (final-accented, marked penult, default penult) and the tendency of Arabic loans to take default penultimate accent. No Shimaore-specific rule.
